summary: Shows how the BGP community attribute can make routing policy easier to set up for customers connected to several providers. It is an informational example of how to use communities, not a new protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1998 describes how customers can tag BGP route announcements with community values. A provider can use a shared mapping from those values to LOCAL_PREF settings instead of maintaining special settings for each customer.

subtitle: An example of using BGP communities to apply routing preferences to customer routes.

tldr.problem: Providers may need customized BGP LOCAL_PREF settings for customers with multiple connections, creating configuration and management work.
tldr.mechanism: A provider maps agreed community values to LOCAL_PREF values, then applies a uniform configuration; customers tag the routes for which they request a preference.
tldr.outcome: The memo describes this as a way to reduce provider-specific configuration and let customers apply policy at prefix rather than only AS level.

facts.label: AS number in the described format

today: RFC 1998 is an Informational memo published in August 1996, and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo describes a community-based BGP configuration technique and reports its use with several customers at that time.

sections.title: The Configuration Problem
sections.content:
A customer connected to more than one provider may want routes handled differently for backup or other routing strategies. The memo says providers commonly customize BGP LOCAL_PREF settings to support these arrangements, and that repeated customer-specific changes can create management and scaling problems.

Providers often configure preferences by Autonomous System (AS), rather than by individual IP prefix. RFC 1998 describes using the BGP community attribute as an alternative that can reduce provider-side customization and allow customer route announcements to carry the requested policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Customers with several network connections may want different routes to receive different preferences. The memo proposes letting customers label routes so providers do not need a separate configuration for each customer.

sections.title: BGP Communities as Route Labels
sections.content:
The BGP community attribute is optional and transitive, and contains a set of four-octet values. In the format described by the memo, the first two octets contain an AS number and the remaining two are defined by that AS. A community groups destination prefixes that share an attribute, and a destination can belong to multiple communities.

Routers can use community membership when making routing decisions. The memo also names NO_EXPORT and NO_ADVERTISE as well-known communities with predefined meanings.
sections.plainLanguage: A BGP community is a value attached to a route. A provider can recognize that value and apply the routing preference agreed for it.

sections.title: Mapping Communities to Preferences
sections.content:
The customer and provider first agree which community values correspond to particular LOCAL_PREF values. The provider then applies a uniform configuration that recognizes those values and sets the matching preference. A customer seeking a preference tags its route announcements with the agreed community.

The memo says customers can choose tags based on AS-path lists or IP-address access lists. This approach can provide route-level customization without requiring the provider to maintain a separate configuration for each customer.
sections.plainLanguage: The customer and provider agree on what each community means. The customer adds the agreed label to a route, and the provider's shared rule sets its preference.

sections.title: MCI's Example Mapping
sections.content:
The memo describes MCI's use of LOCAL_PREF values for customer routes, customer backup routes, other ISP routes and customer-provided backup routes. It presents community values 3561:70, 3561:80 and 3561:90 mapped to LOCAL_PREF values 70, 80 and 90, respectively. The memo says the default LOCAL_PREF value in the described network was 100.

Customers could select the community for a route using an AS-path list or an IP-address access list. The authors report that the technique had been tested and was in use with several customers, and that MCI was migrating other customized configurations to the uniform approach.
sections.plainLanguage: In the example, each community value maps to a LOCAL_PREF value. Customers choose the label for a route, and the provider applies the corresponding setting.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's security considerations section states that security issues are not discussed in the memo. It presents a routing-policy configuration technique using the BGP community attribute and LOCAL_PREF, without specifying additional security mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not discuss security issues.
